Glucose enters the cells via GLUT 2 (a tissue specific transporter) and is then transported to the liver where it is converted into glycogen. This glycogen is then released back into the bloodstream in order to regulate blood sugar levels. If there is too much glucose in the bloodstream, GLUT 4 will be used to store it as fat.  The normal range of blood glucose is between 4-7mmol/l. It is important that this level does not drop below 4mmol/l or else the brain will stop functioning. When blood glucose levels are low, the pancreas releases insulin which regulates the amount of glucose in the bloodstream by stimulating the uptake of glucose into cells. Insulin also encourages the storage of glucose as fat. Wrist drop is a common symptom of radial nerve damage. It occurs because the muscles that extend the wrist are supplied by the deep branch of the radial nerve, and cannot contract to support the weight of the arm. This results in the wrist dropping down towards extension. Loss of sensation in the lateral side of the forearm is due to the median nerve. However, loss of sensation in the anterior of the forearm (regardless of the side) is due to the superficial branch of the radial nerve - this branch innervates all of the skin over the posterior surface of the hand. Therefore, it is most likely that both the radial and the superficial branches of the radial nerve have been damaged. MDMA is commonly known as ecstasy or molly.  It is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor SNRIs which prevents the uptake of these two neurotransmitters. Serotonin is responsible for mood and emotional regulation and norepinephrine is associated with the 'fight or flight' response so it increases alertness. It also causes release of large amounts of dopamine which is associated with pleasure.  The side effects are due to depletion of the serotonin levels which can cause anxiety. The toxic effect of MDMA is due to over activity of the sympathetic system which leads to vasoconstriction and hypertension (high blood pressure). This is why Steve experiences symptoms such as thirst and increased urination.  As the drug wears off the serotonin levels begin to recover and this reduces the pleasurable feelings and increases anxiety.  Risk factors for serotonin syndrome are use of other serotonergic drugs (e.g antidepressants) and if polypharmacy is involved. Symptoms of serotonin syndrome are agitation, confusion, diarrhoea, muscle rigidity, rapid heart rate, seizures, shivering and sweating.  Treatment is to discontinue the medication and observe for recovery. If there is evidence of increasing serotonin syndrome then cyproheptadine is used to reduce serotonin levels. This is an antihistamine however it also blocks serotonin receptors.  Patients should be monitored for 24 hours.  Further management depends on whether there is organ involvement i.e cardiovascular or respiratory.  For example if the patient goes into a coma then they will need IV fluids, vasopressors and mechanical ventilation. Ibuprofen is a NSAID (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug), these work by inhibiting the COX domain of PGHS which stops production of prostaglandins. They are reversible competitive inhibitors as they block the active site of the enzyme. The other two options would also stop the activity of the enzyme but aren't competitive inhibitors. An irreversible inhibitor permanently changes the shape of the enzyme so it cannot bind to substrate again. A non-competitive inhibitor binds to an allosteric site of the enzyme, changing the enzyme's shape but not the active site, meaning that the substrate can still bind to the enzyme. This means that there will be a reduced rate of reaction but the Vmax will remain the same. An example of this kind of inhibition is the inhibition of phosphofructokinase by ATP. The reason why this is important is because we need to know that these drugs have an effect on all cells in the body. This is a problem if you take them at high doses or for long periods of time as they have a negative impact on the stomach lining and kidneys. There are safer alternatives such as paracetamol which only acts on the central nervous system.   Source: Medical Biochemistry by Baynes and Dominiczak, Chapter 7 - Cell signalling and drugs. puberty is controlled by a complex interaction between GnRH, LHRH, GH, IGF-1 and sex steroids (oestrogens and testosterones). It is controlled by a 'central timing mechanism' that controls the onset of pubertal changes at around the same age in all children. This central timing mechanism is set by factors such as nutrition, stress, environment etc.  The major hormonal event that signals puberty to begin is a rise in levels of testosterone or estrogen. These sex steroids stimulate the HPG axis. The HPG axis consists of the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland. In girls, it is FSH secreted from the anterior pituitary that acts on the ovarian follicles and causes them to develop. When one of these mature follicles ruptures, oestrogen levels rise. Oestrogen then acts back onto the hypothalamus and pituitary gland to cause GnRH release. GnRH then causes LH release. LH then stimulates ovulation and further oestrogen production. In boys, testosterone acts on leydig cells in the testes, causing LH release. LH then stimulates leydig cell development and testosterone production. So basically, GnRH is only released when there are sufficient levels of oestrogen or testosterone. If we look at Helena's question, we see that she wants to know how growth spurts occur. We know that growth spurts are caused by GH release. GH is released in 'pulsing' amounts, meaning sometimes it will be high and other times low. It is thought that this 'pulsing' release of GH is what allows tissues to grow at different rates and therefore cause growth spurts. Therefore, the correct answer is E. Urinary urea is usually excreted unchanged by the kidneys. When renal function is impaired, urea blood levels rise (uremia). Urea is non-toxic in small amounts but large amounts can cause coma and death. Plasma urea concentration is related to renal function. Normal ranges are 10–48 mmol/L. In acute renal failure, urea rises rapidly. It then plateaus at a level that depends on the degree of renal damage. The plateau value is related to the GFR. A urea clearance <10% of creatinine clearance indicates an irreversible renal disease.  From Case 6 - Renal Lecture - Acute Kidney Injury and Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy.  Symptoms of uraemia:- Nausea- Vomiting- Abdominal pain- Headaches- Fatigue- Malaise- Asthenia- Altered mental state- Irritability- Insomnia- Restlessness- Muscle cramps- Paresthesias- Coma- Death- Lethargy- Anxiety- Tachypnea- Tachycardia- Hypertension- Hypotension- Bradycardia  Clinical manifestations of uremia depend on the plasma urea concentration. Mild uremia occurs when the plasma urea concentration is between 25 and 75 mM. At this stage, patients may have no symptoms or only slight nausea and vomiting. Moderate uremia occurs when the plasma urea concentration is between 75 and 300 mM. Patients with moderate uremia experience more severe nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, fatigue, malaise, and irritability. Severe uremia occurs when the plasma urea concentration exceeds 300 mM. Patients with severe uremia may present with altered mental status, insomnia, restlessness, muscle cramps, paresthesias, coma, lethargy, anxiety, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypertension, hypotension, bradycardia, and even death. Saturated fatty acids contain no C=C double bonds therefore are straight and don't bend as easily. This makes them suitable for making solid fats like margarine and shortening. They are also hydrophobic (repelled by water) so they form a barrier to prevent water loss. Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more C=C double bonds which means they have a kink in their structure. They are liquid at room temperature because they can rotate around the C=C bonds. They are also hydrophilic (attracted to water) so they dissolve in water. Omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids both have a C=C double bond at the start of the chain. Omega-9 fatty acids do not have any C=C double bonds at all. These properties make unsaturated fatty acids useful for controlling cholesterol levels and fighting disease.  In cyclohexane, the six carbon atoms form a ring shape. There are no double bonds between the carbons but there are two methyl groups attached to each carbon atom. Cyclohexane is a saturated compound because it contains no double bonds.  In ethene, the two carbon atoms share a double bond. Ethene is an unsaturated compound because it contains a double bond.  It’s important to note that a molecule doesn’t need to be a fatty acid to be saturated or unsaturated. For example, ethanol is an alcohol molecule which contains seven carbon atoms. The first and last carbon atoms form a methyl group, and the second and sixth carbon atoms form a methylene group. The other four carbon atoms form a ring shape. Ethanol is an unsaturated molecule because it contains a double bond between the second and sixth carbon atoms. 4 major proteins involved in regulating the movement of Ca2+ into and out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). Pericarditis: inflammation of the pericardium that surrounds the heart. Can be caused by a viral infection such as hep B or tuberculosis or it can be idiopathic. Symptoms include malaise, chest pain on bending, shortness of breath, pericardial friction rub and pulsus paradoxus. ECG shows PR depressions and ST elevations. TNF-alpha release from macrophages causes fibrosis and thickening of the pericardium which restricts cardiac movement resulting in reduced cardiac output and congestive heart failure. Treatment includes diuretics to reduce fluid build up and corticosteroids to reduce inflammation. Pericarditis can lead to constrictive pericarditis which is a chronic condition that results in irreversible cardiac tamponade. It is characterised by constrictive pericardium, absent friction rub, absence of pleural effusion and persistent raised JVP. Aortic dissection - Sudden and severe central crushing chest pain that radiates to neck, back or abdomen. Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with the presence of an excess amount of depolarisng current (Phase 3 prolonged) due to long QT syndrome or other pathological conditions.  Amiodarone has been linked to the induction of Torsade de Pointes in patients.  It is a class III drug used to treat VT and AF. This patient has respiratory acidosis because he is hypoxemic and the pO2 is low. His pH is less than 7.46 indicating acidosis. He also has a high CO2 level which could be due to hypoventilation or hypercarbia due to the acidosis. If it was hypercarbia due to the acidosis then the CO2 would have been lower as it would have been counteracting the acidosis. HCO3- is normal so there is no metabolic acidosis. Therefore the condition is respiratory acidosis which is compensated by metabolic alkalosis.  Compensation is seen in the BE which is high and the pH is close to normal.  The fact that the pH is only slightly raised from normal indicates that this is early stages of compensation. If the pH had been more normal then the body's compensation would not be working as well.  Raising the O2 concentration does not improve the condition.  This patient should have his oxygen therapy optimised and if possible a cause for his hypoventilation treated.  A ventilator may be needed.  The underlying condition causing this patient to be hypoventilating could be chronic lung disease, chest wall deformity or neuromuscular problems.  It is important to identify these causes and treat them appropriately.  Respiratory acidosis can lead to coma and death so it is important that this patient receives appropriate treatment.
